title: What is HTML?
summary: HTML gives a webpage its content and structure.

subtopics.title: Elements
subtopics.explanation:
An element marks content and its role. `

Hello

` creates a paragraph: the tags surround its text. It is like a labeled container for one kind of content. Browsers build a document tree from elements and use that structure when displaying the page. In practice, a heading names a section, while a paragraph holds related sentences. In a real page, use a heading and paragraphs to structure an article before choosing colors.

subtopics.title: Tags
subtopics.explanation: Tags are the angle-bracket labels around an element name. Many elements have an opening tag and a closing tag; some are void elements and do not wrap content. It is like opening and closing a box around an item. Learn the element’s syntax so nesting is correct. In practice, an anchor navigates; a button performs an action in the current interface. In a real page, a link with an href can be opened or copied using normal browser behavior.

subtopics.title: Attributes
subtopics.explanation: An attribute adds information to an element. An image uses `src` for its file and `alt` for a text description; a link uses `href` for its destination. It is like adding labeled fields to a container. Use only attributes that fit the element and quote their values. In practice, a form label gives its input a name that can be announced by assistive technology. In a real page, a form label names its input even when the visual layout changes.

subtopics.title: Semantic meaning
subtopics.explanation: A semantic element describes its job. A `<button>` is for an action; an `<a>` is for going somewhere. It is like choosing a tool by its purpose. Meaningful elements provide built-in keyboard and accessibility behavior that a generic styled box does not. In practice, cSS can change a semantic element’s appearance without changing its HTML meaning. In a real page, a button activates an action and includes familiar keyboard behavior.

subtopics.title: The browser
subtopics.explanation: The browser reads HTML and builds a document structure that it can display and expose to assistive tools. CSS changes appearance, and JavaScript can respond to interaction. It is like a house frame, paint, and working doors. Keep structure meaningful before adding visual styling. In practice, use the browser accessibility tree to inspect what roles and names are exposed. In a real page, inspect the accessibility tree to verify the browser understands the chosen element.

foundations.overview: HTML is the language used to structure content on the web. It marks headings, links, images, buttons, and other parts so browsers can present them and assistive tools can describe them. Think of HTML as the frame of a house: CSS decorates it, while JavaScript can add behavior. Choose elements by meaning, then style them.
foundations.whyItMatters: Meaningful HTML gives the browser and assistive technology a useful structure. It also supplies familiar interaction behavior that would otherwise need custom code.
foundations.mentalModel: HTML is the language used to structure content on the web.
commonUseCases: Structure an article with a heading, paragraphs, and lists.
Create links and buttons with their native browser behavior.
Label images and form fields so their meaning is available beyond appearance.
Build a semantic article or help page.
Create a form with labeled controls and a submit action.

commonMisconceptions.myth: HTML is responsible for all page behavior and styling.
commonMisconceptions.reality: HTML describes structure and meaning; CSS styles it and JavaScript adds behavior.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A generic div is equivalent to every semantic element.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Buttons, links, headings, and landmarks provide meaning and built-in behavior a div does not.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If the page looks right, its HTML structure is correct.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Visual appearance cannot prove that the document outline, keyboard use, or accessible names are sound.

visualExplorer.title: From markup to a tree
visualExplorer.caption: The browser parses your HTML tags into a tree of nodes (the DOM): the html element contains head and body, which contain headings and paragraphs.

interactiveExamples.title: Your first HTML
interactiveExamples.explanation: A few tags is all it takes. Notice the angle brackets never show up — the browser turns each tag into structured, rendered content.

files.index.html:
Hello, web!

This is my first HTML page.

HTML describes the structure of content.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A large heading 'Hello, web!' followed by two paragraphs, with the word 'first' shown in bold.

interactiveExamples.title: HTML structures, CSS styles
interactiveExamples.explanation: The same HTML can look completely different with CSS. HTML provides the meaning; CSS provides the look. Try imagining this without the styles.css file — same content, plain appearance.

files.index.html:
Same HTML

Structure is HTML. Appearance is CSS.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A dark-themed page with a cyan heading and light paragraph text — same markup, different look thanks to CSS.

codeLab.title: Mark up plain text
codeLab.instructions:
This page has raw, unmarked text. Wrap the first line in an

heading and each remaining line in its own

paragraph so the browser knows their meaning.

files.index.html:
My Cooking Blog
Welcome to my site about food.
I post a new recipe every week.

codeLab.expectedOutput: A heading 'My Cooking Blog' followed by two separate paragraphs.

files.index.html:
My Cooking Blog

Welcome to my site about food.

I post a new recipe every week.

hints: The main title of a page is an <h1>.

Each block of running text is a

element with an opening and closing tag.

keyTakeaways: An element marks content and its role.
Tags are the angle-bracket labels around an element name.
An attribute adds information to an element.
A semantic element describes its job.
The browser reads HTML and builds a document structure that it can display and expose to assistive tools.
